segments.text: A molecule in your saliva. In a minute, it does what would otherwise take at least a million years.

segments.text: Crackers are packed with starch. Zoom right in, and starch turns out to be a chain. Hundreds, even thousands, of glucose molecules, linked end to end. Glucose is a sugar, but locked up in a chain like this, it doesn't taste sweet.

segments.text: And those links are tough. Leave one in water at room temperature, and on average it would last millions of years.

segments.text: Enter amylase: an enzyme made in your salivary glands. It's a carbohydrase: it snips starch into smaller sugars, like maltose, which is just two glucose units joined together. And maltose does taste sweet.

segments.text: That's what an enzyme is: a biological catalyst. It speeds up a reaction without being used up or changed. Nearly every reaction in your body has one, whether it's building things up or breaking them down.

segments.text: Without enzymes, your metabolism would be far too slow to keep you alive. Nearly all enzymes are proteins: long chains of amino acids, folded into a precise shape. And that shape is everything.

segments.text: Every enzyme has a small pocket called the active site. The molecule it works on, the substrate, fits inside, forming an enzyme–substrate complex. Held there, a bond becomes much easier to break. Snap. The products leave, and the active site is free for the next one.

segments.text: The active site is complementary to the substrate: not the same shape, but a perfect fit. The enzyme is the lock. The substrate is the key.

segments.text: That's why enzymes are specific. Each one only fits its own substrate. Amylase can't even digest paper. It's mostly cellulose, another chain of glucose, but its links are joined differently, so it just doesn't fit.

segments.text: Lock and key is a brilliant model, but it's a simplification. Real enzymes aren't rigid. As the substrate binds, the active site moulds itself around it. That more accurate picture is called induced fit. For GCSE and IGCSE, lock and key is all you need. Induced fit is an A-level idea. Just remember: it's a model, not a photograph.

segments.text: Which brings us to myth number one: that enzymes get used up. They don't. After each reaction, the enzyme is unchanged, ready to go again, and again. And some are astonishingly fast. Catalase is found in almost all your cells. One molecule of it can break down hundreds of thousands of molecules of hydrogen peroxide. Every second.

segments.text: Your cells do replace old enzymes, eventually. But the reaction itself never uses them up.

segments.text: Now, temperature. Molecules are always jiggling around. Heat them up, and they gain kinetic energy. They move faster. Enzymes and substrates bump into each other more often, and with more energy.
segments.ttsText: Now, temperature. Molecules are always jiggling around. Heat them up, and they gain kinetic energy. They move faster. Enzymes and substrates bump into each other more often, and with more energy.

segments.text: So more collisions are successful, with the substrate landing in the active site. More enzyme–substrate complexes form, and the rate goes up. Up to a point, warmer means faster. The temperature where the rate peaks is called the optimum. For many enzymes in your body, it's around 37 degrees: body temperature.

segments.text: Here's what actually happens. The rate crashes, and it doesn't recover.

segments.text: An enzyme's shape is held together by lots of weak bonds. Too much heat, and it vibrates so violently that those bonds break. The chain unravels, the active site loses its shape, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme has been denatured.

segments.text: It's the same kind of change that turns egg white solid in a hot pan. You can't uncook an egg, and cooling usually won't fix the enzyme either.

segments.text: Cold is different. Molecules have less kinetic energy, so there are fewer collisions. But the enzyme isn't denatured. Warm it up, and it recovers.

segments.text: And that's myth number two: that heat "kills" enzymes. Enzymes were never alive. An enzyme is a molecule, a very clever one, but it can't die. It's denatured. Its active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits, and no enzyme–substrate complex can form. In an exam, that's the answer that gets the marks.

segments.text: pH, how acidic or alkaline something is, can denature enzymes too. Too far either way, and the bonds holding the active site in shape are disrupted.
segments.ttsText: P H, how acidic or alkaline something is, can dee-nature enzymes too. Too far either way, and the bonds holding the active site in shape are disrupted.

segments.text: So every enzyme has an optimum pH. Amylase, in your mouth, works best close to neutral, around pH 7. Your stomach is strongly acidic, often around pH 2. And pepsin, a protease that digests protein there, works best right around that. Different enzymes, tuned to different places.

segments.text: So, back to that cracker. As you chew, amylase meets the starch. The chains slot into its active site, and it snips them into maltose, over and over, without being used up. Your mouth is about 37 degrees, and close to neutral. Just right. Links that would last a million years or more on their own? Broken while you chew. That sweet taste is you, tasting enzymes at work.
